idiom_name: plain mixins + typing.Protocol, with __init_subclass__ for subclass-time hooks
implementation_notes: Python has no compile-time type parameters and dispatch happens through the MRO at call time, so a base class cannot be given 'the derived type' during compilation; a runtime self-reference (type(self), cls in classmethods, or a TypeVar bound in stubs) is the closest analogue and is checked only statically by type checkers. The mixin half is served by ordinary multiple inheritance, and PEP 487's __init_subclass__ lets a base validate, register or decorate every subclass at definition time - the modern replacement for the base-level metaclass machinery that class-creation hooks used to require - while structural interfaces are expressed with typing.Protocol. CRTP's goal (vtable-free polymorphism) is not a Python decision at all: choose protocols/ABCs for interfaces, mixins for shared behaviour and __init_subclass__ for hooks.
pitfalls: __init_subclass__ is not called for the class that defines it, only for its subclasses, so a base that must itself be registered needs an explicit decorator or a separate call.

Class-statement keyword arguments are routed to __init_subclass__; a subclass that does not forward **kwargs to super() breaks cooperative multiple inheritance in ways that only appear when another mixin is added.
Protocol-based typing is static only: isinstance() needs @runtime_checkable (and then checks only member presence), and none of it guarantees the concrete behaviour at runtime.
alternative: Ordinary mixin classes with type hints plus typing.Protocol/abc for interfaces, and __init_subclass__ (PEP 487) when a base must register, validate or configure its subclasses at class-creation time; method resolution is dynamic and deliberately so.
